questions.question:
The statement [latex]( eg p)\Rightarrow ( eg q)[/latex] is logically equivalent to which of the statements below?
I. [latex] p\Rightarrow q [/latex]
II. [latex]q \Rightarrow p [/latex]
III. [latex]( eg q)\vee p[/latex]
IV. [latex]( eg p)\vee q[/latex]
questions.explanation:
[latex] eg p\Rightarrow eg q[/latex] is the contrapositive of [latex]q\Rightarrow p[/latex], so they are equivalent (II). Also [latex]a\Rightarrow b\equiv eg a\vee b[/latex], so [latex] eg p\Rightarrow eg q\equiv p\vee eg q[/latex] (III).

I ([latex]p\Rightarrow q[/latex]) and IV ([latex] eg p\vee q[/latex]) are the converse, which is different.

Answer: II and III only

questions.question:
Consider the first-order logic sentence [latex]F:\forall x(\exists yR(x,y))[/latex]. Assuming non-empty logical domains, which of the sentences below are implied by F?
I. [latex]\exists y(\exists xR(x,y))[/latex]
II. [latex]\exists y(\forall xR(x,y)) [/latex]
III. [latex]\forall y(\exists xR(x,y))[/latex]
IV. [latex]\neg \exists x(\forall y\neg R(x,y))[/latex]
questions.explanation:
F: every x has some y with R(x, y).
- I: [latex]\exists y\exists x R(x,y)[/latex] follows (the domain is non-empty) True
- IV: [latex]\neg\exists x\forall y\neg R(x,y)\equiv\forall x\exists y R(x,y)[/latex], which is F itself True
- II (one y for all x) and III (every y is hit) do not follow.

Answer: I and IV only

questions.question:
A sender S sends a message m to receiver R, which is digitally signed by S with its private key. In this scenario, one or more of the following security violations can take place.

I. S can launch a birthday attack to replace m with a fraudulent message.
II. A third party attacker can launch a birthday attack to replace m with a fraudulent message
III. R can launch a birthday attack to replace m with a fraudulent message.

Which of the following are possible security violations?
questions.explanation:
A birthday attack finds two messages with the same hash. Only the signer S can use it: S signs a harmless message and later claims the signature was for the other one with the same hash. A third party or R cannot create S's signature on a new hash.

Answer: I only

- If [latex]L_f[/latex] is recursive: on input x, try y = each string of B* in order and test x#y with the decider; since f is total, the correct y is found and the search halts [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] f is computable.

questions.question:
Recall that Belady's anomaly is that the pages-fault rate may increase as the number of allocated frames increases. Now consider the following statements:

Which of the following is CORRECT ?

options.B: S1 is true, S2 is false
options.C: S1 is false , S2 is true
options.D: S1 is false, S2 is false

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Random replacement can evict an unlucky page in the bigger memory, so faults can increase with more frames [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S1 TRUE.

Answer: S1 is true, S2 is false

questions.question:
In a database system, unique time stamps are assigned to each transaction using Lamport's logical clock . Let TS([latex]T_{1}[/latex]) and TS([latex]T_{2}[/latex]) be the timestamps of transactions [latex]T_{1}[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}[/latex] respectively. Besides, [latex]T_{1}[/latex] holds a lock on the resource R, and [latex]T_{2}[/latex] has requested a conflicting lock on the same resource R. The following algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks in the database system assuming that a killed transaction is restarted with the same timestamp.

Assume any transactions that is not killed terminates eventually. Which of the following is TRUE about the database system that uses the above algorithm to prevent deadlocks?

options.A: The database system is both deadlock-free and starvation- free.
options.B: The database system is deadlock- free, but not starvation-free.
options.C: The database system is starvation-free but not deadlock- free.
options.D: The database system is neither deadlock- free nor starvation-free.

questions.explanation:
If the requester T2 is older (smaller timestamp), the younger holder T1 is killed; otherwise the younger requester waits. So a transaction only ever waits for an older one: no cycle of waits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock-free.

A killed transaction restarts with its old timestamp, so it keeps getting older relative to new ones and eventually becomes the oldest, which is never killed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] starvation-free.

Answer: both deadlock-free and starvation-free

questions.question:
Consider a 2-way set associative cache with 256 blocks and uses LRU replacement, Initially the cache is empty. Conflict misses are those misses which occur due the contention of multiple blocks for the same cache set. Compulsory misses occur due to first time access to the block. The following sequence of accesses to memory blocks.

(0,128,256,128,0,128,256,128,1,129,257,129,1,129,257,129)

is repeated 10 times. The number of conflict misses experienced by the cache is ___________.
questions.explanation:
128 sets (2-way). Blocks 0, 128, 256 map to set 0; 1, 129, 257 map to set 1. Set 0 sees 0, 128, 256, 128, 0, 128, 256, 128 each round:
- Round 1: 0, 128, 256 are compulsory misses; then 0 and 256 miss again (conflict) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 conflict misses.
- Each later round: 0 and 256 keep evicting each other (128 stays) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 conflict misses.

Set 0: 2 + 9 [latex]\times[/latex] 4 = 38. Set 1 behaves the same: 38. Total = 76

Answer: 76
